newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says will use line-item veto sparingly.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says will use line-item veto sparingly.

text.p: President Clinton said Monday he might use the line-item veto to excise some spending items from a $95 billion tax bill he will sign Tuesday.
Clinton told reporters White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles was leading an intensive review to see if there were any items that would be appropriate for the line-item veto.
"I think if we have it, it ought to be used. I believe that it ought to be used somewhat sparingly," he said in a picture-taking session in the Oval Office.
Clinton said his experience as governor of Arkansas, where he had similar authority over state spending, showed "once I used it a few times I didn't need to use it very much anymore."
The president was scheduled to sign the legislation Tuesday. Clinton has five days after the signing to act.

The bill was passed by both houses of Congress last Thursday, the first tax bill to face the possibility of such a veto. The line-item authority allows the president to strip items from spending and tax measures without vetoing an entire bill.
The Supreme Court dismissed a legal challenge to the law in June on technical grounds so the line-item veto still is expected to face a court fight in the future.

Under the line-item veto law, Congress must identify for review tax breaks that apply only to a limited number of taxpayers. The congressional Joint Committee on Taxation has identified 79 such provisions.

One example is a tax break approved for New England producers of hard cider. Instead of being taxed at the same $1.07-a-gallon rate as wine, cider with an alcohol content below 7 percent would be taxed at 22.6 cents per gallon, less than half of what is charged for its major competition, beer.
Another example was the export credit that Microsoft and other computer software makers won for overseas sales.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the review of whether to use the line item veto on aspects of the budget began over the weekend.
He would not speculate on whether Clinton would use the authority.

Asked if he expected Clinton to to know by the Tuesday signing whether he plans to use the line item veto, McCurry replied: "No." Asked if Clinton was being briefed on the issue Monday, he replied: "No. Not that I know of."
Congress can override any line-item veto by a two-thirds majority in each house.
